A Need For Conceptual Science What About Biology Chemistry

Aug 8, 2016 • Janice Cotcher

“Chemistry open day” by UCLmaps is licensed under CC BY 2.0

D’Arcy Thompson began his book On Growth and Form by quoting Immanuel Kant: “chemistry was a science, but not a Science. . . for that the criterion of true Science lay in its relation to mathematics.” [3] Thompson went on to explain how chemistry was elevated to the level of Science, whereas biology had not yet reached that level. Today this is not longer the case: biology is changing and becoming more quantitative. Collecting data and obtaining results (however quantitative) are commonly part of science, but are not science itself.

Stark differences between mathematics and science are clearly demonstrated in biology. For example, evolution is a successful theory, but there is no way to prove that the theory of evolution is correct in a mathematical sense. Mathematics is a language that develops its own internal structure through proving theorems. Mathematics and statistics do not use the methods of the empirical sciences. Focusing on formalism, truth, and proof thus misinforms students about science. Understanding the concepts in science is a first step in clarifying this; understanding the role of mathematics in science is a second. [2]

For mathematics to make sense, science should make sense first. The issue has two interrelated aspects: They are the understanding of science and the understanding of mathematics for science. [2] In biology, as with the other sciences, understanding orders of magnitude are one of the greatest hindrances to understanding. In his reflection on the innumeracy among biologists, Dr. Roger Brent, President and Director of the Molecular Sciences Institute, states

Not infrequently, such follow-up questions establish the point that the student is at least a little bit uncomfortable with powers of 10, let us say, the difference among 100,000, 1 million, 10 million, 108, and 1011. A friend has suggested that this behavior is not discomfort with powers of 10 so much as discomfort at the idea of being asked to make numerical estimates. [1]

Citations

[1] G. Gigerenzer and A. Edwards. Simple tools for understanding risks: from innumeracy to insight. Bmj, 327(7417):741, 2003.

[2] I. Karsai and G. Kampis. The Crossroads between Biology and Mathematics: The Scientific Method as the Basics of Scientific Literacy. Bio-Science, 60(8):632-638, 2010.

[3] D.W. Thompson. On growth and form. On growth and form., 1942.
